items.prompt: Describe the defining actions of abrasion, deflation and attrition by wind.
items.canonical_answer: Abrasion uses moving grains to wear a target surface. Deflation removes loose material from the ground. Attrition wears transported grains as they collide with one another.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the abrasion action step; 1 for removal in deflation; 1 for load-particle collisions and their wear result.

items.prompt: Explain the error in calling grain-to-grain corner loss “abrasion of a rock face”. What contact would distinguish the processes?

items.prompt: Describe the selective-removal sequence that can create a desert pavement in a deflation model.

items.prompt: Describe suspension, saltation and surface creep as wind-transport movements.
items.canonical_answer: Suspension carries particles within the air. Saltation moves grains in repeated short hops with landings. Surface creep rolls or slides grains along the ground.

Describe the transport modes shown in this path diagram, using the airborne, hopping and ground-contact paths.
items.canonical_answer:
A stays in the air at every time and never touches the surface, which supports suspension. B repeatedly lifts off, travels a short arc and lands again, which supports saltation. items.prompt: Describe a sequence by which wind can build a sand dune.
items.canonical_answer: Wind transports available sand. A local reduction in transporting conditions or an obstacle allows some grains to accumulate. The deposit alters airflow and further deposition and redistribution can build a mound or ridge.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the first sand-transport step; 1 for trapping or local deposition; 1 for accumulation/redistribution as the dune-building result.

items.prompt: Describe the star-dune interpretation: an original Sossusvlei teaching sketch has four ridges meeting around a central peak; the long-term wind record includes several directions.
items.canonical_answer: The ridges form a multi-armed plan around a central high area, which supports a star dune. Because the long-term winds blow from several directions, each wind pushes sand back towards the centre, so the dune mainly grows upward rather than migrating steadily in one direction and each arm keeps its own slip face.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the radial-ridge pattern; 1 for the central-peak/arm evidence; 1 for linking form to the supplied multi-directional regime.

items.prompt: A teaching record from the dune belt near Swakopmund shows a sand ridge 800 m long and 40 m wide, lying parallel to several similar ridges. A long-term wind record shows strong winds from one direction for most of the year and from a direction about 120° away at other times. Describe what the record shows about the type of dune and how it formed.
items.canonical_answer: The ridge is very long compared with its width (800 m ÷ 40 m = 20:1) and lies parallel to similar ridges, so it is a seif (linear) dune. The two winds each pile sand onto one flank, so instead of moving forward as a crescent the ridge grows in length along the resultant direction of sand transport, which depends on the strength and duration of the winds.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the feature: an elongated 20:1 ridge identified as a seif/linear dune; 1 for the evidence of parallel neighbouring ridges; 1 for the interpretation that winds from two directions build the ridge lengthways along their average direction.

items.prompt:
A supplied resource records A as four ridges radiating from a central peak, B as a crest 800 m long and 40 m wide, and C as a bare patch whose fines leave downwind while the ground lowers 15 cm.
(a) Name the process removing fines at C. [1]
(b) Describe the form and classification contrast between A and B. [3]
(c) Describe two observations at C that support a hollow-forming interpretation. [2]
(d) What judgement is supported about whether one present-day wind arrow proves the long-term regime that made A? [1]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Deflation. (b) A has radiating arms around a centre, consistent with star; B is elongated with a 20:1 ratio, consistent with linear. (c) Fine loss and measured surface lowering support excavation. (d) No: one current direction does not establish the long-term multi-directional regime.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for deflation.
(b) 3 B marks for A’s radial form, B’s elongated proportional evidence and the correctly contrasted classifications.
(c) 2 B marks for the fine-removal and lowering data, both interpreted as evidence of excavation.
(d) 1 C mark for a supported decision rejecting one current arrow as proof of the long-term regime.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that increasing gravel cover proves new gravel was added? At a hypothetical site, cover increases from 40% to 70%; collectors record fines leaving downwind; repeated images identify the same coarse fragments and no gravel input is recorded. Judge the explanation of the observed surface change, recognising the limits of the observation. [5]
items.canonical_answer: Disagree with proof of addition. The surface can become more gravel-dominated when fines are removed, so higher cover need not require added stones. Fine loss and the repeated identification of coarse fragments support residual concentration through deflation. The observations do not rule out every unrecorded input, but addition is not established; removal is the supported explanation for the stated interval.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for judging the cover-percentage evidence, fine-removal mechanism, repeated-fragment record and limitation concerning unrecorded inputs. Reward causal reasoning rather than unrelated lists of wind processes.
1 C mark for a supported decision that increased cover alone does not prove addition.
